chapter_title: A Catechumen asked the Apostle: When I would give an Offering to the Saints, shall I inflict a Wound on the Alms?
chapter_note: This kephalaion is dominated by the Q&A frame plus institutional/pastoral concerns (catechumen → elect alms-offering; anxiety about “sinning” against the Living Soul; absolution language; church vocabulary). The extended judge/enemy/doctor analogy functions as moral-pastoral justification for alms preparation rather than a cosmos→cosmos correspondential mapping or a systematic cosmological exposition. No recoverable pre-compilation correspondential substrate can be cleanly extracted here.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Dialogue/question frame marker (“Once again… questioned the apostle”) and explicit institutional setting (catechumen, alms-offering, elect). Although “Living Soul” is cosmological vocabulary, it is invoked in a practical church context (preparing food/offerings), not as systematic cosmology.

Continuation of the catechumen’s question within the Q&A apparatus; framed as personal moral calculus about ‘good’ vs ‘sin’ done to the Living Soul—an institutional/pastoral problem statement rather than substrate exposition.

Pastoral reassurance/exhortation (“Do not be frightened…”) aimed at alms practice; cosmos→institution application (alms-making as healing). The opening attribution (“When the apostle heard… he spoke”) is compilation frame, but the paragraph’s substance is pastoral direction, not core cosmological mapping.

Extended legal/violence analogy (enemy, judge, punishment) used to set up moral reasoning. The imagery stays in human social institutions (court/judge), not cosmic architecture; it serves pastoral argumentation in response to an institutional alms question.

Doctor/knife/healing analogy—classic moral-pastoral motif (hurt to heal). No systematic degree-structure, no cosmos→cosmos correspondential correlations; functions to justify necessary ‘harm’ in practice.
Completion of the medical analogy with honor/gifts; still moral illustration in service of institutional instruction, not an older cosmological teaching sequence.

Explicit application of the analogy to alms-offering and the Living Soul; includes institutional means of ‘healing’ (“elect, psalms and prayers and blessings”). This is directly cosmos→contemporary church practice, a key marker of later pastoral application.
Fragmentary continuation of the ‘other person’/assailant side of the analogy; still moral-legal rhetoric tied to harm against the Living Soul, not substrate cosmology.

Probable editorial seam/extension (as flagged): heavy institutional vocabulary (catechumens, church) and soteriological bookkeeping (absolution, mass of sins, intercessor). This extends the discussion into church discipline/benefits for catechumens—late institutional graft, not mixed.
Institutional generalization to ‘all the catechumens’ performing offerings for the Living Soul; continued church-practice emphasis rather than systematic cosmological exposition.
